content: The field of safety concerning manufactured nanomaterials (MNMs) is advancing rapidly. A research agenda established by Stone et al. in collaboration with stakeholders in 2014 anticipated significant progress in validated measurement methods, exposure route assessments, and monitoring strategies in the short term. Consequently, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) has proposed updating these guidelines in 2022. Manufactured nanomaterials (MNMs) pose potential occupational risks, and various studies and systematic reviews have been conducted to address these concerns. For example, Honner and Grzebyk conducted an occupational survey in five industries in France, highlighting the need for safety measures. The European Commission has also published a working paper on the types and uses of nanomaterials, including safety aspects. The WHO has developed air quality guidelines, with updates in 2000 and 2005, to address global concerns. The Delphi process, a methodology for eliciting expert opinions, has been utilized in guideline development. The GRADE system has emerged as a consensus for rating the quality of evidence and the strength of recommendations, as described by Guyatt et al. and Iorio et al. The International Union of Food, Agricultural, Hotel, Restaurant, Catering, Tobacco, and Allied Workers’ Associations (IUF) and other organizations have released recommendations on the use of nanotechnology in food. The European Trade Union Confederation (ETUC) and the Canadian Union of Public Employees have also addressed nanomaterial safety. Research by Nel et al. has emphasized the importance of alternative test strategies for nanomaterial safety assessment. The National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) has developed a hierarchy of controls to reduce worker exposure. Ellenbecker has highlighted the role of engineering controls as interventions to minimize exposure. Studies have categorized manufactured nanomaterials and proposed approaches for hazard assessment. For instance, Nagai et al. identified the critical factors of diameter and rigidity in multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs) that contribute to mesothelial injury and carcinogenesis. Landvik et al. reviewed criteria for grouping MNMs to facilitate hazard and risk assessment. The European Commission has provided guidance for workers on safely handling manufactured nanomaterials. Training programs, such as those by Kulinoski and Lippy, have been developed to educate workers on nanotechnology risks. The WHO has also addressed the assignment of hazard categories to specific nanomaterials. Systematic reviews have examined occupational exposure limits, measurement techniques, and exposure routes for engineered nanomaterials. For example, Basinas et al. reviewed the forms and routes of exposure, while Debia et al. analyzed reported exposure scenarios. The British Standards Institution (BSI) has published standards for assessing inhalation exposure to nano-objects. Control banding has been explored as a qualitative risk management tool for nanomaterials. Studies by Zalk and Heussen, as well as Eastlake et al., have evaluated its effectiveness. Training health and safety committees to use control banding has been implemented in the United States, as described by Bracker et al. Public expectations and attitudes toward health and safety measures, including annual physical examinations, have been studied. Gulumian et al. conducted a systematic review of screening and surveillance programs to protect workers from nanomaterials. Training programs for workers at risk of exposure to specific nanomaterials have been developed by organizations such as the WHO. The systematic review teams have assessed risks associated with MNMs, occupational exposure limit values, control banding, specific risk mitigation techniques, and health surveillance. These efforts aim to enhance worker safety and prevent risks from exposure to manufactured nanomaterials.
